\chapter{Once More, and Which One}
\label{ch:ka-once-more}
\hlchaptermodality{71}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for another one, ask somebody to repeat themselves, and ask when and which.}

Complete KA-C71-which and say the whole ya- question family in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[innondu]{\kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} (innondu) — another one}

\label{lesson:KA-C71-another}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say what you think about something, out loud.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು}} (\emph{innondu}) — \textquotedblleft{}another one, one more\textquotedblright{}.

Two pieces, both of them yours already: \kn{ಇನ್ನೂ} (\emph{innū}, \textquotedblleft{}still, yet\textquotedblright{}) and \kn{ಒಂದು} (\emph{ondu}, \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}). Push them together and the long vowel shortens: \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು}.

\textbf{\kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} \kn{ಚಹಾ}} (\emph{innondu cahā}) — \textquotedblleft{}another tea.\textquotedblright{} That is what you say when the cup is empty and the answer is yes.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one, and one more}]
Pair it with plain \kn{ಒಂದು} and you have the Kannada way of saying \textquotedblleft{}one … the other\textquotedblright{}:

\textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲಿ}, \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} \kn{ಅಲ್ಲಿ}} (\emph{ondu illi, innondu alli}) — \textquotedblleft{}one here, the other there.\textquotedblright{}

There is no separate word for \emph{the other}. Kannada counts: this one, and the one-more. It is the same trick the language uses everywhere — build the second thing out of the first rather than name it fresh.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second helping, and a way to talk about two things one at a time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ondu}, then \emph{innondu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{innondu cahā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ondu illi, innondu alli}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{innū}, and say what it added to \emph{ondu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mattu} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hēḷu} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{nadi}, \emph{kaṇṇu}, \emph{magaḷu}, \emph{maga}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}another one\textquotedblright{}.) Which two words is it built from? (\emph{innū} and \emph{ondu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[innondu sala hēḷi]{\kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} \kn{ಸಲ} \kn{ಹೇಳಿ} (innondu sala hēḷi) — please say it once more}

\label{lesson:KA-C71-say-again}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: how do you ask for another tea?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} \kn{ಸಲ} \kn{ಹೇಳಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} \kn{ಸಲ} \kn{ಹೇಳಿ}} (\emph{innondu sala hēḷi}) — \textquotedblleft{}please say it once more.\textquotedblright{}

\kn{ಸಲ} (\emph{sala}) is a time in the counting sense — one time, two times — so \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} \kn{ಸಲ} is \textquotedblleft{}one more time\textquotedblright{}. The verb is the polite \kn{ಹೇಳಿ} you met with the sentence about the way.

This is the single most useful sentence a beginner owns, and until now this book had no way to build it. Everything else you can survive without; you cannot survive without asking somebody to repeat themselves.

Put \kn{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು} in front and it is as polite as it gets: \textbf{\kn{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು} \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು} \kn{ಸಲ} \kn{ಹೇಳಿ}}. Said with a slight rise it is warm rather than demanding, and nobody in Karnataka will mind hearing it — a stranger trying the language is worth the second go.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The repair sentence. With it, every other sentence in this book gets a second chance.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{innondu sala hēḷi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dayaviṭṭu innondu sala hēḷi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} somebody says something too fast — ask for it again
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{innondu}, then \emph{ondu illi, innondu alli}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ಮ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{anta} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{kere}, \emph{magu}, \emph{snēhita}, \emph{kuṭumba}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask for that once more? (\emph{innondu sala hēḷi}.) What does \kn{ಸಲ} count? (Times.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yāvāga]{\kn{ಯಾವಾಗ} (yāvāga) — when?}

\label{lesson:KA-C71-when}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: ask somebody to say it once more.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಯಾವಾಗ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಯಾವಾಗ}} (\emph{yāvāga}) — \textquotedblleft{}when?\textquotedblright{}

The question set is nearly complete: who, where, what, why, and now when. This is the last one an everyday exchange keeps reaching for.

\textbf{\kn{ಯಾವಾಗ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತೀರಾ}?} (\emph{yāvāga baruttīrā?}) — \textquotedblleft{}when will you come?\textquotedblright{} Notice the question ending on the end of it, doing the same job it did on \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಾ}.

The answers are already yours: \kn{ಈಗ} (\emph{īga}, \textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{}), \kn{ನಾಳೆ}, \kn{ನಾಡಿದ್ದು} (\emph{nāḍiddu}, \textquotedblleft{}the day after tomorrow\textquotedblright{}). Ask \kn{ಯಾವಾಗ} and you can understand what comes back.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five question words. Who, where, what, why, when — and a reason and an opinion to answer them with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāvāga}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāvāga baruttīrā?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} answer it — \emph{īga}, or \emph{nāḍiddu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yāke}, then say \emph{yāvāga}, and say which one asks for a reason
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{athavā} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ೇ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{beṭṭa}, \emph{sahāya māḍu}, \emph{kēḷu}, \emph{tegeduko}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಯಾವಾಗ} ask? (\textquotedblleft{}When?\textquotedblright{}) Answer it with the word for \textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{īga}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[va]{\kn{ವ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S139-letter-va}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌ೇ} — long or short?

One character this time — and it is standing in the middle of the word for \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{} and the word for \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{} alike.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ವ}}
\textbf{\kn{ವ}} — \emph{va}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{v}, it is \textbf{va}. Kannada's \emph{v} is the same sound that Tamil keeps at the front of many words where Kannada has turned it into \emph{b}, which is why \kn{ಬಾ} and \kn{ಬರೆ} look nothing like their Tamil cousins.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ವ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಯಾವಾಗ}} \emph{yāvāga} — when, from the lesson before this one
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಥವಾ}} \emph{athavā} — or
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೂವು}} \emph{hūvu} — a flower
  \item \textbf{\kn{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು}} \emph{dayaviṭṭu} — please
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ವ}}
Put your pen on \kn{ವ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ವ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಯಾವಾಗ}  ·  \kn{ಅಥವಾ}  ·  \kn{ಹೂವು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ವ} three times, saying \emph{va} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ವ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ವ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{va}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yāva]{\kn{ಯಾವ} (yāva) — which?}

\label{lesson:KA-C71-which}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which character did you trace last, and what does \emph{yāvāga} ask?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಯಾವ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಯಾವ}} (\emph{yāva}) — \textquotedblleft{}which?\textquotedblright{}

It goes in front of a noun, exactly where an adjective goes: \textbf{\kn{ಯಾವ} \kn{ಪುಸ್ತಕ}?} (\emph{yāva pustaka?}) — \textquotedblleft{}which book?\textquotedblright{}

Put it with the word for \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{} and you can finally put a real choice to somebody: \textbf{\kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಅಥವಾ} \kn{ಕಾಫಿ}? \kn{ಯಾವ} \kn{ಪುಸ್ತಕ}?} — offer the two, then ask which. Until this word there was no way to ask anybody to pick.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ya- family, and what each member asks}]
Look at what the last three lessons share. \kn{ಯಾರು}, \kn{ಯಾಕೆ}, \kn{ಯಾವಾಗ}, \kn{ಯಾವ} — a whole family beginning \textbf{\kn{ಯಾ}-}, and each one asks about a different thing: a person, a reason, a time, a choice.

The pointing words came in a set of three beginnings, \kn{ಇ}- for near, \kn{ಅ}- for far, \kn{ಎ}- for the question. \kn{ಯಾ}- is the same idea in its other shape, and Kannada uses the two interchangeably at the front of a question word: \kn{ಏಕೆ} and \kn{ಯಾಕೆ} are one word with two faces.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The question set, closed. Who, what, where, why, when, which — and an ending that turns any statement into a yes-or-no question besides.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāva}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāva pustaka?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāru}, \emph{yāke}, \emph{yāvāga}, \emph{yāva} — the whole family
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{athavā}, then offer a choice and ask which
  \item \emph{Recall:} the whole chapter — \emph{innondu}, \emph{innondu sala hēḷi}, \emph{yāvāga}, \emph{\kn{ವ}}, and this one
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ādare} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nānū} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ēkendare} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{adu nija anta yōcisuttēne} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{dāri}, \emph{haḷḷi}, \emph{bare}, \emph{arthamāḍiko}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಯಾವ} ask? (\textquotedblleft{}Which?\textquotedblright{}) Where does it sit — before or after the noun? (Before.)
\end{tcolorbox}
